subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate I wish to present the viewpoint of one of the representatives of 225,000 Acadians who form about one-fifth of the population of the maritime provinces and who are the direct descendants of the 5,000 Acadians who were expatriated and deported by Governor Lawrence in 1755 and scattered over the uninhabited shores of the Atlantic ocean from Boston to the Mexican border. Gradually these expatriates trickled back to their farms in the land of Acadie, as the poet Longfellow calls it. They settled there and lived under great difficulties; for a century they were considered practically as a conquered people. These people to-day bear no resentment or animosity against anyone for the sufferings which they underwent during that crucial period. They are loyal subjects of the British crown and of the Dominion of Canada, just as loyal as any of their fellow citizens in the maritime provinces or anywhere else in Canada. Unlike our fellow Canadians

whose traditions and loyalties are linked up with the British empire, we Acadians have no European ties except our mother tongue. France practically abandoned us to our fate two centuries ago.
But with our historic background of persecution, expulsion and suffering, we emphasize our opposition to compulsion for overseas service during any war until we have been shown the supreme need for such a measure. We do assert our desire and our right to choose between compulsion and voluntary enlistment for overseas service. In the last war we did our full share under the voluntary system. It is true that we rebelled against conscription, but we rebelled because of the unfair and unjust way in which it was enforced in our peaceful villages. There was bloodshed in our midst, and we do not want a repetition of these atrocities.
We do recognize that the best way to defeat our enemy is to fight him outside of Canada and to prevent him from reaching our shores. To this end we are prepared to give freely of our lives and to the limit of our man-power and of our meagre means. But we want no more guns and no more bayonets tracking down our youth like wild beasts in our hills and our forests. We have open minds, but the way to convince us is not by making us guzzle conscription by ramming it down our throats.
I present the views of a man whose broad mentality is patterned on that of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and on that of the man whom I have succeeded: in this chamber, who was brought up and educated among the Scotch people of Pictou county, Nova Scotia. Like him, next to my religious faith, I place my Canadian citizenship ahead of everything else this side of eternity.
The present debate revolves around two chief topics, conscription for overseas service and the proposed plebiscite. While most of the speakers heard so far, have admitted or applauded the excellence of Canada's war effort as a whole, a -certain minority persist in bitter criticisms of the methods employed by the government to raise man-power for overseas. On this particular point the country and this house are divided into two groups, those who favour voluntary enlistment and those who favour conscription for overseas service.
The advocates of the voluntary system- and they are more numerous than certain newspapers and the Gallup poll would indicate-claim that each individual has the sacred right to determine of his own volition whether or not his life should be exposed to the supreme sacrifice in overseas service outside his native land. They refuse to be

The Address-Mr. Veniot
taken by the scruff of the neck and hurled into foreign fields of battle to forfeit their lives, while the possessors of flat feet and owners of wealth are permitted to go scot-free by certain processes of exemption, as occurred in the last war. They consider themselves justified in saying: "You members of parliament may think it proper to pass legislation regimenting men for overseas service, but it will not be you armchair legislators or members of your families who will endure the hardships, who will do the fighting, who will take the risks and do the dying." Those are words I heard with my own ears not very long ago.
The supporters of voluntary enlistment claim that up to the present time all the requirements of our own forces, army, navy and air force, have been met one hundred per cent. Statements to this effect were made in the house this week by three ministers, the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston), the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie), and very forcefully yesterday by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). Statements to this effect have been made just within the past few days by the commander in chief of the Canadian forces, by no less a person than General McNaughton, when he stated that the Canadian people have met to the hilt all the requirements so far of man-power in England.
Each year since the beginning of the war a programme of man-power has been outlined for overseas service. This programme has been set by the Department of National Defence in consultation with the highest military authorities both in England and in Canada. The extent of the requirements is established in the light of all existing circumstances at the time of the formulation of the plan, and all requirements thus far decided upon have been met to the hilt.
The programme for 1942 has just been announced by the Minister of National Defence. It involves the raising of a considerable number of men, running from 173,000 to
193,000.	This is a large programme, and at the present rate of enlistments there can be no doubt in the mind of any member of this house that we shall again meet all the requirements by voluntary enlistment. At this particular date and without knowledge of what the government further proposes in the way of plans, how can the opposition truthfully say that voluntary enlistment has failed? I need not insist upon the reports which come from the different sections of Canada. I have here reports from New Brunswick published in the Saint John Telegraph-Journal, and here is one
headline: "Surge in army recruiting." And here is a report in the Ottawa Citizen, showing that 500 recruits were signed up in the month of January in the city of Ottawa. Similar reports come from all over Canada. The Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson) a few days ago stated that in the last seven months our enlistments have averaged 20,000 a month, which makes 140,000 in seven months. Why, then, the clamor that the nation's war effort is going to be delayed if not ruined by the proposed plebiscite? Must recruiting in every- part of Canada cease while the plebiscite is on? Are the different military divisions and depots to be closed down and all training suspended during that time? Why make such childish statements to an intelligent public?
It has been frequently and truthfully said in this house that raising an army for overseas service is only one part of an all-out war effort. The methods heretofore adopted for providing men, voluntary enlistment and conscription, are only means to that end. Conscription for that purpose is and will remain of debatable, doubtful value. It may be equitable in certain respects, it may be just in some ways, but it is most provocative and irritating to all elements, and charged with racial dynamite. In fact, I submit, sir, that by the odious way in which it was applied in 1917 by the arch-imperialists of this country, it was transformed into a racial issue. This is a strong statement. Nevertheless it is the bald truth, as I shall proceed to show.
I again reiterate that conscription now is, and always will be, a racial issue in Canada. It was forced into such a place in our thoughts by the unforgivable and unforgettable circumstances with which the Conservative party surrounded the birth of conscription and the way in which it was carried out in the last war, and proposed again in the present war. All of us Canadians must recognize this fact without delay before our national edifice is too far ablaze with passion.
Deep down in his heart every Canadian knows that conscription, more than ever to-day, contains the germs of strife, of division, of violent resistance, and possibly of bloodshed as in the last war. We never shall win this war while w-e are divided by a racial issue, and just now, with passions burning to white heat in certain sections of the country, we are headed for catastrophe.
Unity cannot be maintained by such fiery statements as those of Premier Hepburn when he charged the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) with deliberately trying to set the French against the British through his lieutenant, Mr. Godbout. I do not know the

The Address-Mr. Veniot

nature of the evil spirits which move the premier of Ontario to speak in such a way and make other firebrand statements against the Prime Minister of the nation. None of his violent utterances are in harmony with the fundamental principles of confederation which brought together two peoples of different tongues, different race and different religion.
Any fair-minded person who has studied the history of Canada since its conquest by the British, and who has a knowledge of the background of strife and struggle which took place between these two racial groups during a century of adjustment, realizes what a tremendous undertaking confederation was, and still is. Why does French Canada feel as it does toward conscription?
All of us need in the worst way to dig into history, to learn the facts, to recall the fundamental principles of bonne entente, and review the problem of the relations of French Canada to the rest of the dominion. May I be permitted merely to enumerate a few points in history which all of us should study with the deepest concern.
First, one which I have already mentioned, and which still lingers in the heart and. soul of every Acadian in the maritime provinces, and which is handed down as a tradition from mother to child on her knees-the expulsion of the Acadians in 1755. Has anything ever been done to rehabilitate and to compensate these innocent victims of the racial hate which existed at that time? No further comments are necessary.
Second, the Quebec Act of 1774.
Third, the Constitutional Act of 1791, by which Canada was divided into Upper and Lower Canada.
Fourth, the war of 1812, when French Canada stuck to England and saved this colony for the British.
Fifth, the rebellion of 1837.
Sixth, the union of Upper and Lower Canada in 1841, by which Lord Durham hoped that the French-Canadians could be manipulated into adopting the language and the customs of the English and assimilated by them. These words are related in history verbatim.
Seventh, the Confederation Act of 1867, by which English- and French-speaking Canadians shook hands and agreed to forget their past differences in order to make Canada one of the greatest countries in the world.
Eighth, the War-time Elections Act and the Military Service Act of 1917, of which I shall say more later.
Ninth, the statute of Westminster.
Tenth, the school acts in eight provinces where French-Canadians are a minority group.

Contrast these with the treatment accorded the English minority in the province of Quebec.
The defenders of conscription are loud in their vociferations for equality of sacrifice. Equality of sacrifice in my estimation naturally presupposes equality of citizenship. I ask this house, is there equality of citizenship for the three-quarters of a million French-Canadians who live outside Quebec and who are denied the right of separate schools for the education of their children in their mother tongue?
These are a few of the historical facts. Let us now confront them with certain other facts.
First, practically all Canadians who support conscription for overseas are of British descent.
Second, there is a very large number of Canadians, also of British descent, who oppose conscription, some because it is their intimate conviction; others because, although favouring conscription as a means of raising troops for overseas service, they view it as a racial issue which nearly wrecked Canada in the last war.
Third, practically every Canadian of French descent is irrevocably opposed to conscription; he holds these views as sacred to him as his religion and his mother tongue. May I recall that there are over three and a half million French-Canadians in Canada, of whom, as I have already said, three-quarters of a million reside outside Quebec.
I ask my bon. friends to recall these facts and figures in their moments of calm reflection.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1917 recognized the racial implications of conscription and the dangers which it contained. Since that time, Mackenzie King, Lapointe and their followers have all been of the same opinion. In the session of 1939, the then leader of the opposition, Doctor Manion, was shrewd enough to perceive it, and in 1940 during the election campaign he repeated from one end of the country to the other the statements he had made in the house. I concede to him in all fairness that he was expressing this opinion not as a bait for vote-catching, but because deep down in his soul he knew the implications of conscription as a racial issue and a danger for Canada. The trouble with us all is that up to the present time none of us has had the courage frankly to put this view before the public in its true light. We have avoided the issue. We have neglected to place before the public the true perspective, to call a spade a spade, to derive from it the only logical conclusion to which this fact leads, namely that during a world war crisis such as we are facing to-day the English

The Address-Mr. Veniot
and French elements of our population must come together without delay and arrive at a reasoned understanding on this vital question.
Unfortunately, extremists of both major political parties in this house beclouded the issue when each accused the other of using conscription as a vote-getter in and out of the province of Quebec. I cannot see how the continuance of violent public statements during an election campaign, such as those of the premier of Ontario, which I have already mentioned, are going to help to bridge the gap between the two races. Equally violent utterances in the opposite direction come from the province of Quebec, and will not span the breach. Nor can I see how the presence of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen in this house could have helped in any way to bring about unity of purpose, when all French Canada recalls his share in the framing and execution of the conscription act in the last war. And what an execution that was!
Here may I be permitted to quote words uttered by Hon. II. C. Nixon a few days ago in this connection. Said he:
I believe it would be a national calamity if Arthur Meighen were returned to public life by South York on Monday.
I recall how Canada was divided in 1917 and 1918 by the War-time Elections Act and the Military Service Act, and which were applied in such an iniquitous way that millions of people still see red when they think of it, and not in Quebec alone either. For this condition no man living to-day is more responsible than Mr. Meighen.
There are certain amenities, Mr. Speaker, which peoples as well as gentlemen owe one another, and the things just mentioned are not of the proper taste nor are they suitable to men occupying such high responsibility in a dual nation like ours, where susceptibilities are always so keen. Fortunately there always exists a great measure of tolerance and fair-mindedness in this country. I have discussed this thorny question of conscription with many of my numerous friends of British origin. Here are the views of a distinguished gentleman, a non-Catholic clergyman with whom I had the pleasure of travelling on the train when returning from the funeral of the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe. He told me that personally he considered the conscription of all man-power the most equitable way of raising troops for overseas if it could be harmoniously carried out. With his knowledge of the historical background of Canada's different peoples he could not conceive of the possibility of any such utopia, and he opposes conscription in the interests of Canadian unity 44561-334
because he regards it essentially as a racial issue fraught with extreme danger to the solidarity of the nation. Never before had it entered my mind that conscription could have such an implication and it was the expression of this thought that made it enter my mind, namely, that conscription in Canada at the present time has become a racial issue. In his estimation, to force conscription would split the nation asunder and ruin our otherwise splendid war effort.
In further discussion he expressed other opinions. Here are some of them. Conscription, according to him, would never be thought of as a method of raising troops in south Africa. Why? Because there also it would be a racial issue between the Boers and the British. In Ireland it would be a religious issue between the north and the south. In Australia, where the population is 97 per cent of British origin, Prime Minister Hughes on two different occasions in the last war called a referendum on this question; on both occasions the measure was thrown out, and the feeling against the prime minister at that time for his conscriptionist view was so strong that, as you know, he had to resign his position as prime_ minister.
At the present date there is no conscription for overseas service in Australia. Are we Canadians any the less British or any the less patriotic than the Australians? In the United States there is no racial cleavage. There, conscription, such as they are imposing it, is purely a matter of policy or expediency. In line with these thoughts, I should like to call the attention of the house to a little book which appeared some time ago entitled "Canadian Peoples," by Mr. B. K. Sandwell, in which he shows the entire historical background of some of the thoughts I have been expressing in this house. The views of this man are those of many broad-minded and informed English-speaking Canadians with whom I have discussed this thorn in the side of our nation.
Conscription as enforced in the last war was recognized as a national blunder and failure as a man-power-producing measure, by the leaders of all political parties, immediately before and during the last election. All Liberal supporters have always proclaimed its failure from the very beginning. The then National Conservative leader, Doctor Manion, as I said, spoke in the house against conscription and, as I have already mentioned, repeated the same speech from coast to coast
The futility of conscription for producing men in numbers is demonstrated by the following figures, some of which were given last week by the Minister of Pensions and
The Address-Mr. Veniot

National Health. The first class of unmarried men from 20 to 34 years of age, registered in 1917, numbered 404,000. Of these, there were 380,000 exemptions claimed for one reason or another, leaving only a difference of 24,000 men to come under arms. By the end of March, 1918, in Ontario, 118,000 claimed exemption and 104,000 exemptions were approved. In Quebec, 108,000 out of 115,000 called received exemption. By the end of March, 1918, in the whole dominion, 31,000 men had been called up of whom 5,000 had defaulted. At the end of the war, as the Minister of Pensions and National Health pointed out a few days ago, only 83,000 men were enrolled under the act, but there was something which the minister did not say. Of this number 22,000 were released on farm leave or on compassionate leave. In the final analysis, 61,000 men formed the total contribution of conscription to the last war effort.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, is this an effort that is worth while, produced by a measure which certain interests are seeking to impose upon Canada to-day? Yet, in spite of this evident failure, in spite of the futility which I have just shown; in spite of the disruption which it caused to national unity; in spite of the hatred which it engendered, the spectre of conscription hovers over this house again to-day as the battlecry of the Conservative party and the ultimate and only means of saving this nation. To cap the climax, the same party calls in as the standard-bearer of conscription the one man in Canada whose very name is anathema to the province of Quebec and wherever there exists in Canada a group of Canadians of French descent-the very man who in 1917 framed the War-time Elections Act and the Military Service Act and saw to their application in the province of Quebec in the odious and provocative manner which all of us recall so well and so sorrowfully.
That wound still bleeds in Quebec. Can members of the Conservative party sincerely believe that their choice of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen last fall as their leader was a tactful one in these difficult times when unity of purpose and harmony and unstinted cooperation of al! classes and creeds and races are more important than gold and guns? Do hon. members opposite honestly think that they can heal Quebec's wounds and many other injuries of the last war by selecting as their chief the very man who inflicted those wounds and who is regarded as the personification of intolerance?
I say that the choice of the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen at that time was a direct challenge to the province of Quebec-

speechtext:
I submit that this choice at such a time, when spirits were aready heated up, was the greatest political strategic error since confederation, which may lead even yet, although the Right Hon. Mr. Meighen was defeated, to dire consequences for the nation. Shortly after the selection of the Right Hon. Mr. Meighen as leader of his party was announced, one of my Conservative friends said to me, "Bennett wrecked the Conservative party by his autocracy, and now Meighen comes to bury it."
As I view the deliberate, gradually worked up conscription agitation, the main object of it seems to be to pit the province of Quebec against the rest of the nation, as a political move the sinister objective of which is to wreck the Liberal party. Only last Thursday the Otthwa Citizen seemed to gloat already over its victim in an editorial saying:
Collapse is bound to come on parliament hill. The signs of disintegration are already to be seen. While the ship of state is being attacked from without by the most terrible forces of barbarism, Canada is being scuttled internally by party politics.
The evil spirits which inspire and guide the backers of conscription at the present time seoin to say weirdly: "If we can create a clamour sufficiently strong to stampede a certain number of English-speaking Liberals into supporting conscription, and thus split the Liberal fold, potential victory and power is ours. Perish unity, perish the nation, so long as the Liberal party and King are destroyed 1"
If this allegation be denied, and no doubt it will be-I do not -blame my friends of the opposition for denying it, because it is a terrible indictment-then I would ask my hon. friends to prove their honesty and sincerity, their love of country, their desire for peace and unity, by considering the generous suggestion made in this house on January 29 by one of their own party, the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Bruce) when he proposed to exclude Quebec from the operation of compulsory selective service. The same thought was expressed on February 9 by the hon. member for Oomox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) when he said, as reported on page 40S of Hansard:
If necessary, I would agree to conscription which would leave out sections where the feeling was anti-conseriptionist. That was done in Ireland twice, during the great war and in this war. No trouble resulted, no ill feeling, and no discrimination. Possibly it would be a good idea here.
As I previously remarked, nearly one-third of the dominion's population is made up of Canadians of French descent, and three-quarters of a million of these reside outside

The Address-Mr. Veniot
of the province of Quebec. I presume that the magnanimous suggestion of the hon. member for Parkdale would include these latter in the scope of his intentions, for to a man, this part of the population is opposed to conscription for overseas service. On every other single point of any all-out total war effort every French-Canadian in this country is in complete harmony with his fellow citizens, as Premier Godbout proclaimed some time ago, and is prepared to go to the very limits of sacrifice in order to win this war.
On the other hand, as I have already pointed out, the absolute totality of the advocates for conscription are of British origin. Upon these, then, I presume the hon. member for Parkdale would impose conscription for overseas service, preserving the system of voluntary enlistment for all Canadians of French descent. May I congratulate the hon. member for having had such a brilliant thought and making such a magnanimous gesture of friendship. It certainly is one of the finest statements I ever heard in this parliament or outside of it, and he has the unqualified blessing of every mother's heart in French Canada.
Yes, Mr. Speaker, give the French-Canadians more of their own commanding officers whose language they understand, more of their own training centres, where they can be taught the intricacies of military technique in their own mother tongue. Can you see the leader of the opposition training in a military school where French is the only language in use? Give them, I say, their own regiments, their own battalions under the voluntary system, and you will see the old French spirit of valour and chivalry showing this nation and the whole world that French-Canadians are not slackers-as I have heard it said within the very walls of this building. They will show that they can repeat many times over the numbers and the valiant deeds of the crack Royal 22nd French-Canadian regiment. They will show that their love of Canada is equal to, if not greater than, that of any other group of Canadians in this country.
We do not seek to shirk our obligations, but we demand respect for the convictions that we hold as deeply rooted in our souls as our religious faith. Barring this one point of conscription for overseas service, we are ready for any sacrifice. Aye, we welcome it, and there is no limit to our possibilities.
I challenge the opposition to support their fellow member in his suggestion. If this were done I should like to see side by side battalions composed of conscripts and of volunteers from the province of Quebec.
I quote the following passage from the Montreal Standard of January 24:
The basis of Canadian confederation, the union of two peoples of different tongue is compromise; the art of effecting compromises that will preserve the unity of Canada has become the chief measurement of Canadian statesmanship. Without the spirit of compromise, the historians of the future will likely find the mixed federation of peoples and institutions that are bound together in the Dominion of Canada would dissolve.
This, Mr. Speaker, explains Baldwin and Lafontaine, Macdonald and Cartier, Laurier and Fielding, King and Lapointe. Such compromise establishes the law of fair exchange in mutual friendship, mutual understanding and agreement, without which this country cannot continue to exist, upon which the survival of the nation is based.
Will some wise man tell the country why such dual leadership has ceased to exist in the Conservative party since the last war? Will someone name the French associates of Borden, Bennett, Meighen, comparable to those of their predecessors, and say why there is not one single Conservative of French extraction in the present parliament, and why there was only one in the last? The hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy) found the atmosphere bitterly cold during the short time he sat on the Conservative benches. Why has French Canada no outstanding representative in the Tory party to-day? Because this party in the last war and since that time ignored the lesson of true statesmanship, given heretofore by the leaders of both major political parties, former leaders whose names will- go down in history as the foster-fathers of union and harmony between the two great races of Canada, while Borden, Meighen and Bennett will be relegated to the background because they ignored the important fact that by their own machinations conscription in Canada will always remain a race issue, whatever their views to the contrary now may be.
Personally, I am prepared to support the proposed plebiscite, and to ask my people to back it up one hundred per cent; not that I favour conscription, but because I feel that a middle course can be worked out which will be just and equitable and less disruptive than conscription as it was and is still conceived by the Conservative party; because I have the utmost confidence in my chief and in his government; because I know that their judgment will be exercised with the utmost caution in the light of all existing circumstances-war conditions, economic conditions and racial difficulties-if and when the moment, of supreme danger arises for the safety of our country and of our allies.
If conscription ever did become a supreme necessity and I could be persuaded of this necessity I would rather see its enforcement
The Address-Mr. Veniot

in the hands of the Prime Minister, noted for his moderation and his broadness of views, and the men surrounding him, than in the hands of the men who made conscription such a flop by the odious way it was enforced in Quebec during the last war.
I submit that there can and must be found some middle course between the two extreme views which now split the country on the issue of conscription. Men of moderate views from aW parties and from both racial groups must get together somehow and calmly study the situation from its every angle. The handwriting of disaster is all too plainly emblazoned on the ceiling over our heads. A truce must be called on the question. The nation's interest is greater than that of the Liberal, the Conservative or any other party at the present time; for if conscription in its 1917 form is put into effect, even at the hour of supreme danger, even as remotely as a year or two hence, I dare not say what will take place in my county and in other sections of the country, unless other means than those of the past are used to persuade the people.
These are terrific things to say, but no sane man can ignore any longer the rumblings that reach us from the cities as well as from the back settlements in opposition to conscription, since Meighen relaunched it as his supreme war cry on November 13 last. Let me quote, in conclusion, a paragraph by Leslie Roberts in a recent issue of Saturday Night-.
It can be said that war in the Pacific rather than tending to change French Canada's attitude to conscription, has stiffened Quebec's determination to have nothing to do with the idea. There continues to be a complete lack of comprehension in hundreds of thousands, possibly millions of English-Canadians' minds as to the root cause of this opposition. Basically, it must be charged to the poorest piece of political and journalistic salesmanship in our history, coupled with a determination on the part of a few editors and orators to cram conscription down Quebec's throat no matter what happens. You do not change the opinions of a democratic minority that way. You merely stiffen their determination not to be browbeaten, and sooner or later, if the process continues, Donnybrook ensues.
Fortunately there are many English-Canadians of this writer's type, educated Canadians who have studied the fundamentals of racial, ethnical economics, who do not let themselves be carried away by passion, whose reasoned outlook on the present situation will help to preserve unity and harmony among our peoples.
May divine providence enlighten a greater number of such minds, chasten our hearts of the bitterness which has welled up during the past three months, and infuse into our souls the kindly balm of mutual tolerance.
